listening.passage:
Lecturer: Electric cars are not a new invention. In the early 1900s, almost one third of American cars were electric. Cheap oil and mass production of petrol engines then pushed them aside.
Their modern revival is based on advances in battery technology. Charging infrastructure remains the biggest barrier: electricity networks and charging stations are insufficient. Researchers aim to increase battery density and shorten charging times. The main future change will be in the growing share of renewable energy supplying the cars, rather than in the cars themselves.

are green because of chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis.

some trees, sugars trapped in the leaves produce red pigments. Finally, the tree seals off
the leaf, and it falls. So the bright colors of autumn are really a sign that the tree is
preparing for winter."

I see Tom's point that not every student needs a second language, but I agree with Sara
that it should be required. Learning another language does more than help with
careers; it trains the brain to think in new ways and builds respect for other cultures.
For example, in my school, students who studied English early found it much easier to
use online resources and connect with people abroad. While it is true that some
students may struggle, schools can offer different levels so no one is left behind.
Making a language optional often means those who would benefit most never try it.
Overall, I believe a required — but flexible — language program prepares students best
for a connected world.

Нина: Зөвшөөрөх хэрэгтэй. Мэдээлэл хурдан хайж, тэмдэглэл авч болно.
Омар: Санал нийлэхгүй. Утас анхаарал сарниулж, лекцэд төвлөрөхийг бууруулдаг.

explanation.en:

Both Nina and Omar make fair points, but I lean toward Omar's view with one
adjustment. It is true that phones can be useful for quick research, as Nina says.
However, in my experience, the temptation to check messages during a lecture is very
strong, and even a short distraction breaks concentration. For example, when my class
banned phones during discussions, students participated far more actively. That said, a
complete ban may be too strict. A reasonable rule would allow phones only when the
professor asks students to look something up, and otherwise keep them away. This

Carlos makes a valid point that working can reduce study time, but I mostly agree with
Emma that a part-time job is worthwhile if it is limited. A few hours of work each week
teaches responsibility, time management, and communication — skills that classes
rarely cover. For example, a friend of mine who worked part-time at a café became far
more confident and organized. The key, however, is balance. If a student works too
many hours, Carlos is right that grades can suffer. In my opinion, a small job of ten to
fifteen hours a week gives students the benefits Emma describes without the harm
Carlos fears. Moderation makes the difference.

prompt.en: What mainly causes ocean tides?
prompt.mn: Далайн түрлэгийг голчлон юу үүсгэдэг вэ?

listening.passage:
"Let's look at why the ocean has tides. Tides are mainly caused by the gravitational pull of
the moon. As the moon orbits the Earth, its gravity pulls on the ocean water closest to it,
creating a bulge — a high tide. Interestingly, there is a second high tide on the opposite
side of the Earth at the same time, caused by the way the Earth itself is pulled toward the
moon. As the Earth rotates, different areas pass through these bulges, which is why most
coasts experience two high tides and two low tides each day. The sun's gravity also plays a
smaller role, especially when the sun and moon line up."

Peter raises a fair concern about honesty, but I side with Yuki that long-term projects
often measure understanding better than exams. A timed exam mainly tests how much
a student can memorize under pressure, while a project shows whether they can apply
knowledge, solve problems, and think independently. For instance, in my science class,
a term-long research project taught me far more than any single test. However, Peter is
right that projects can be copied. The solution is not to abandon them but to design
them carefully — with progress checks and individual presentations that make copying
difficult. In my view, a mix of both methods would be ideal, but projects deserve a much
larger role than they have today.
